newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S., Canada sign protocol on social security tax.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada sign protocol on social security tax.

text.p: Canada and the United States signed an agreement on Tuesday changing the way they tax social security benefits as well as some capital gains from real estate, the Canadian Finance Department said.

The protocol to their joint tax treaty will give the country of residence the exclusive right to tax social security benefits, with better-off citizens probably paying more than before and lower-income residents paying less.

Canada will tax U.S. Social Security benefits paid to Canadian residents, eliminating the 25.5 percent automatic withholding tax that the United States had applied. And Canada will tax only 85 percent of those benefits.

This will mean lower taxes for some Canadian residents who are in a lower tax bracket, but appeared to mean others could be hit with a higher bill, since top tax brackets are above 50 percent in Canada. Even if only 85 percent is taxed, the top rate is still well above the original 25.5 percent.

The United States will also now be able to tax Canadian Pension Plan and Old Age Security benefits -- which had been subject to a 25 percent charge -- at normal income tax rates, which can be higher than that but are well below levels in Canada.

The two countries had caused numerous complaints when they started the current system, whereby the paying country withholds taxes, at the beginning of 1996. Before that, the country of residence had the right to tax the benefits but half of that was entirely tax-free.

The protocol also provides that Canadian residents who invest in U.S. real estate through Canadian companies will continue to pay Canadian tax, rather than any possible future U.S. tax, when they sell their shares, and vice versa.
The protocol must be ratified by the U.S. Senate and the Canadian Parliament.
